analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey puts AI use among educational services firms, NAICS 61, at 35.5% in the latest period, up from 33.8% in the prior period. The measure counts firms that answered yes to using AI in the last two weeks, so it captures recent operational use rather than experimentation or planned adoption.

The U.S. Department of Education's AI use-case inventory shows the agency itself deploys AI for transcription through Otter.AI, writing assistance through Grammarly, and foundation model applications through AWS Bedrock for text generation, summarization, conversational AI, personalization, and content creation. The inventory also lists internal uses such as generating code snippets, converting county names to FIPS codes, creating mock data sets, training employees on prompt engineering, and drafting outreach strategies and job qualifications.

The World of AI's course catalog lists 13 AI courses, 11 of them free and 3 with public companion code. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285, and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry providers including DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai, and Andrej Karpathy. The catalog notes that all ten courses tracked offer free access to core materials, with three pairing that with paid certificate options or public code repositories, but it does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken.

HolonIQ describes itself as a market intelligence platform for the global impact economy, with capabilities to size addressable markets, forecast scenarios, map partnerships, and track competitive landscapes for governments, institutions, technology companies, and investors. The excerpt does not report specific education AI funding totals or vendor market shares. The Department of Education's inventory describes expected benefits such as cost reduction and productivity gains for CAISY, time savings for Otter.AI, and writing quality improvements for Grammarly, but it does not provide measured return on investment figures.

The Department of Education frames its AI work around responsible and secure usage, citing adherence to federal regulations and an executive order on removing barriers to American leadership in artificial intelligence. Its inventory includes testing data loss prevention filters by feeding AI fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information. For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the available evidence is strongest on adoption and federal internal use cases, while sector-wide ROI, vendor concentration, and course completion outcomes remain unreported in these sources.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
